title: Cut the VAT registration threshold to £30,000
headline: Cut the VAT threshold from £90,000 to £30,000 over four years: RF’s £2bn.
description: Businesses register for VAT once their turnover passes £90,000, about double the OECD average. Firms bunch just below it and hold back growth to stay there. The Resolution Foundation proposes cutting the threshold to £30,000 over four years and puts the yield at £2 billion. HMRC costs the whole threshold, the relief for everyone below it, at £3.1 billion in 2025-26, so RF’s figure for most of the way down is in proportion. Held flat in cash here, which overstates the early years of a four-year phase-in.

baselinePolicy.text: Businesses must register for VAT if their taxable turnover is more than £90,000; HMRC costs the threshold at £3.1 billion in 2025-26.

source.quote: Businesses have to register for VAT if their VAT taxable turnover is more than £90,000

terms.label: The Resolution Foundation’s yield from cutting the VAT registration threshold to £30,000 over four years
terms.unit: £ million a year once the cut is complete

source.quote: reducing the threshold to £30,000 over the next four years, raising £2 billion

rawSource.note: RF’s end-state figure held flat in cash from the start year. RF phases the cut over four years, so the early years would raise less; HMRC’s £3.1bn cost of the whole threshold (relief row vat-ns14) is the scale check.

caveats: RF’s figure for the full cut, applied from the start year; RF would phase it over four years, so 2027-28 would raise much less than shown.

A scale check, not a certification: HMRC’s static cost of the whole threshold is £3.1 billion in 2025-26 (relief row vat-ns14), and RF’s £2 billion for cutting it two thirds of the way is consistent with that. Nobody in government has costed the cut.
Compliance, not just yield: over a million more traders would register, file and charge VAT; the OBR has written about the bunching the threshold causes.

considerations.text: Some newly registered firms would pass VAT on to customers, some would absorb it, and the bunching just below £90,000 would move down to £30,000; RF’s figure is a central estimate on a static base.
Small traders with turnover between £30,000 and £90,000 and their customers pay: sole traders, small shops and services that are outside VAT today.
HMRC would take on more than a million new VAT registrations; the cost of collecting from very small firms is high relative to the tax.

interactions.text: A higher standard rate raises what every newly registered trader charges; the two compound.
